units.text: ⟦0⟧5 Line addressing⟦1⟧ ¶⟦2⟧⟦3⟧
units.sourceHTML: 5 Line addressing ¶

units.text: An address represents the number of a line in the buffer. ⟦0⟧ maintains a ⟦1⟧current address⟦2⟧ which is typically supplied to commands as the default address when none is specified. When a file is first read, the current address is set to the address of the last line of the file. In general, the current address is set to the address of the last line affected by a command.
units.sourceHTML: An address represents the number of a line in the buffer. ed maintains a current address which is typically supplied to commands as the default address when none is specified. When a file is first read, the current address is set to the address of the last line of the file. In general, the current address is set to the address of the last line affected by a command.

units.text: One exception to the rule that addresses represent line numbers is the address ‘⟦0⟧’ (zero). This means "at the beginning of the buffer", and is valid wherever it makes sense.
units.sourceHTML: One exception to the rule that addresses represent line numbers is the address ‘0’ (zero). This means "at the beginning of the buffer", and is valid wherever it makes sense.

units.text: An address range is two addresses separated either by a comma (‘⟦0⟧’) or a semicolon (‘⟦1⟧’). The value of the first address in a range cannot exceed the value of the second.
units.sourceHTML: An address range is two addresses separated either by a comma (‘,’) or a semicolon (‘;’). The value of the first address in a range cannot exceed the value of the second.

units.text: In a semicolon-delimited range, the current address (‘⟦0⟧’) is set to the first address before the second address is calculated. This feature can be used to set the starting line for searches if the second address contains a regular expression. The address ‘⟦1⟧’ (zero) is valid as a starting point so that ‘⟦2⟧’ can match ⟦3⟧ in the first line of the buffer.
units.sourceHTML: In a semicolon-delimited range, the current address (‘.’) is set to the first address before the second address is calculated. This feature can be used to set the starting line for searches if the second address contains a regular expression. The address ‘0’ (zero) is valid as a starting point so that ‘0;/re/’ can match re in the first line of the buffer.

units.text: Addresses can be omitted on either side of the comma or semicolon separator. If only the first address is given in a range, then the second address is set to the given address. If only the second address is given, the resulting address pairs are ‘⟦0⟧’ and ‘⟦1⟧’ respectively. If a ⟦2⟧-tuple of addresses is given where ⟦3⟧ > 2⟦4⟧, then the corresponding range is determined by the last two addresses in the ⟦5⟧-tuple. If only one address is expected, then the last address is used. It is an error to give any number of addresses to a command that requires zero addresses.
units.sourceHTML: Addresses can be omitted on either side of the comma or semicolon separator. If only the first address is given in a range, then the second address is set to the given address. If only the second address is given, the resulting address pairs are ‘1,addr’ and ‘.;addr’ respectively. If a n-tuple of addresses is given where n > 2, then the corresponding range is determined by the last two addresses in the n-tuple. If only one address is expected, then the last address is used. It is an error to give any number of addresses to a command that requires zero addresses.

units.text: A line address is constructed as follows:
units.sourceHTML: A line address is constructed as follows:

units.text: The current line (address) in the buffer.
units.sourceHTML: The current line (address) in the buffer.

units.text: The last line in the buffer.
units.sourceHTML: The last line in the buffer.

units.text: The ⟦0⟧th line in the buffer, where ⟦1⟧ is a number in the range ‘⟦2⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: The nth line in the buffer, where n is a number in the range ‘0,$’.

units.text: The ⟦0⟧th next line, where ⟦1⟧ is a non-negative number.
units.sourceHTML: The nth next line, where n is a non-negative number.

units.text: The ⟦0⟧th previous line, where ⟦1⟧ is a non-negative number.
units.sourceHTML: The nth previous line, where n is a non-negative number.

units.text: The next line. This is equivalent to ‘⟦0⟧’ and may be repeated with cumulative effect.
units.sourceHTML: The next line. This is equivalent to ‘+1’ and may be repeated with cumulative effect.

units.text: The previous line. This is equivalent to ‘⟦0⟧’ and may be repeated with cumulative effect.
units.sourceHTML: The previous line. This is equivalent to ‘-1’ and may be repeated with cumulative effect.

units.text: The first through last lines in the buffer. This is equivalent to the address range ‘⟦0⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: The first through last lines in the buffer. This is equivalent to the address range ‘1,$’.

units.text: The current through last lines in the buffer. This is equivalent to the address range ‘⟦0⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: The current through last lines in the buffer. This is equivalent to the address range ‘.;$’.

units.text: The next line containing the regular expression ⟦0⟧. The search wraps to the beginning of the buffer and continues down to the current line, if necessary. The suffix ‘⟦1⟧’ is a GNU extension which makes ⟦2⟧ match ⟦3⟧ in a case-insensitive manner.
units.sourceHTML: The next line containing the regular expression re. The search wraps to the beginning of the buffer and continues down to the current line, if necessary. The suffix ‘I’ is a GNU extension which makes ed match re in a case-insensitive manner.

units.text: The previous line containing the regular expression ⟦0⟧. The search wraps to the end of the buffer and continues up to the current line, if necessary. The suffix ‘⟦1⟧’ is a GNU extension which makes ⟦2⟧ match ⟦3⟧ in a case-insensitive manner.
units.sourceHTML: The previous line containing the regular expression re. The search wraps to the end of the buffer and continues up to the current line, if necessary. The suffix ‘I’ is a GNU extension which makes ed match re in a case-insensitive manner.

units.text: The apostrophe-x character pair addresses the line previously marked by a ‘⟦0⟧’ (mark) command, where ‘⟦1⟧’ is a lower case letter from the portable character set ‘⟦2⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: The apostrophe-x character pair addresses the line previously marked by a ‘k’ (mark) command, where ‘x’ is a lower case letter from the portable character set ‘[a-z]’.

units.text: Addresses can be followed by one or more address offsets, optionally separated by whitespace. Offsets are constructed as follows:
units.sourceHTML: Addresses can be followed by one or more address offsets, optionally separated by whitespace. Offsets are constructed as follows:

units.text: ‘⟦0⟧’ or ‘⟦1⟧’ followed by a number adds or subtracts the indicated number of lines to or from the address.
units.sourceHTML: • ‘+’ or ‘-’ followed by a number adds or subtracts the indicated number of lines to or from the address.

units.text: ‘⟦0⟧’ or ‘⟦1⟧’ not followed by a number adds or subtracts 1 to or from the address.
units.sourceHTML: • ‘+’ or ‘-’ not followed by a number adds or subtracts 1 to or from the address.

units.text: A number adds the indicated number of lines to the address.
units.sourceHTML: • A number adds the indicated number of lines to the address.

units.text: It is not an error if an intermediate address value is negative or greater than the address of the last line in the buffer. It is an error if the final address value is negative or greater than the address of the last line in the buffer. It is an error if a search for a regular expression fails to find a matching line.
units.sourceHTML: It is not an error if an intermediate address value is negative or greater than the address of the last line in the buffer. It is an error if the final address value is negative or greater than the address of the last line in the buffer. It is an error if a search for a regular expression fails to find a matching line.
